baseline_incident_edges.relationship: Makes the historical concept of childhood a problem for family history, while prompting disputes over sources and generalization.
baseline_incident_edges.evidence_note: The formulation retains Pollock’s distinction between concept and affection and her source criticism (1983 excerpt pp. 1–10, especially 2 and 6–9). It neither endorses Ariès’s chronology nor reassigns later writers’ stronger claims to him.

baseline_incident_edges.relationship: Historicizes familiar family institutions and social attitudes, opening comparative questions between modernity and earlier arrangements.
baseline_incident_edges.evidence_note: Attributed to Jean-Claude Chamboredon, 1985 pp. 150–151, on the work’s sociological questions and the family/death studies. This is a named reader’s substantive assessment, not a claim that Ariès belonged to a single sociological school.

baseline_incident_edges.relationship: While accepting Le Goff’s medieval cultural turning point, Ariès argues that his focus on purgatory as a place understates enduring older beliefs in repose and waiting (1983).
baseline_incident_edges.evidence_note: Printed pp. 153–156. Ariès accepts the terminus ad quem and cultural significance. His diffusion discussion allows regional variation and revises his own earlier late dating; this is no blanket denial of Le Goff’s thesis. French book (1981) not independently read.

baseline_incident_edges.relationship: Credits Ariès’s study of childhood and family life as an important model of historical inquiry.
baseline_incident_edges.evidence_note: Own2010 retrospective441 names L’enfant et la vie de famille dans la France d’Ancien Régime and calls it a masterpiece while acknowledging criticism of it. Admiration is not converted into agreement with every thesis or a formal teaching relation. Complete original book and criticisms unread.

baseline_incident_edges.relationship: Brewer uses Ariès’s account of criticism of progress moving from the Right toward the Left to explain interest in preindustrial societies and mentalities.
baseline_incident_edges.evidence_note: Own2010 printed93 attributes the claim to Ariès, mediated in n27 by Ginzburg’s1993 Microhistory p20. No direct Ariès work/title or original reading established; the mediated route is explicit, not a formative influence claim.

relevant_group_routes.relationship: Childhood and family as historical subjects
relevant_group_routes.evidence_note: The demography umbrella's strand on childhood evidence (Ariès; Pollock) and its household studies can be read alongside Canadian childhood and family history, which grew from social and family history (Parr, ed., 1982; Bradbury, ed., 1992) more than from family reconstitution. PhD context: 12 of 132 PhDs engaging this group cite Ariès (9% vs 3%; lift 2.96). Comparison; no descent from Ariès is asserted.
